title: The Thirty Years' War
hook: Europe tears itself apart until the Peace of Westphalia

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Bartholomew's Day and the Huguenots, a wedding that ended in a massacre. Your line was never in his name.

In Prague, an angry crowd of Protestant nobles storms into a castle room, grabs royal officials, and throws them out of a high window. The officials survive the fall. The story goes that Catholics said angels had caught them, while their enemies said they'd landed in a heap of dung. Either way, nobody laughed for long. That window opened onto a war that would grind on and on across German lands: armies coming and going and coming back, Catholic and Protestant rulers on both sides, and plenty of soldiers fighting mainly for pay.

It started as a quarrel about religion and rights in Bohemia. It didn't stay there. Kings and princes joined in for faith, for land, for power, and the lines blurred: Catholic France ended up backing Protestant armies against the Catholic Habsburgs. The religious labels stayed on the banners, but the reasons kept multiplying. And the kings didn't pay. Villagers did, in the path of armies that lived off the land, taking food, burning farms, leaving hunger and sickness behind. Then, slowly, came the end. Diplomats gathered in two towns in Westphalia, in northwest Germany, Catholics in one and Protestants in the other, and the talks dragged on. Out of them came the Peace of Westphalia. It didn't make anyone agree about God. It set terms for living side by side: Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed rulers were all recognized, and Europe began, unevenly, to step back from fighting wars over which church was right. Peace at last, but a tired peace, bought at a terrible cost. The prophet Isaiah describes a different ending, in the King James Bible: "they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more." Westphalia wasn't that. Treaties never quite are. But it was a step back from the edge. And Jesus' words sit beside any peace table: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God."

Choose one place where fighting hasn't ended, and look for the people working to stop it: a negotiator at a long table, a medic, a neighbor sharing bread across a line. Breathe in and let one of them come close; breathe out and wish them strength for the slow work. If you pray, pray for them in your own words or rest with blessed are the peacemakers; if you don't, keep them in your attention and wish their place peace at last.
Westphalia. The peace treaty that ended the Thirty Years' War, letting Catholic and Protestant rulers live side by side without agreeing about God.
Your line: peace at last. A tired peace is still a peace. Day eight hundred eighty-one, done.

howItsDone: Christians in different churches pray for places at war in their services and at home, and the beatitude 'blessed are the peacemakers' is one they may read when they do.
